why: Canary 1.1 is at parity with stable 1.0 on every signal in the dashboard, with no error or latency regression. Errors: 0 5xx and 0.00% err% on 2411 canary requests, same as stable (0 5xx on 7374). Exposure is real and as designed: canary served 2411/9785 = 24.6% of traffic, matching the expected ~25% for 1 canary pod behind 3 stable pods, so the clean result is not an artifact of the canary being starved of traffic. Aggregate latency is effectively identical: p50 34 vs 34, p95 93 vs 94, p99 105 vs 104 (canary vs stable). Per-endpoint parity holds where it matters most: /browse p50/p95 22/27 on both; /search 47/59/61 identical on both; /checkout 82/104/107 vs 81/103/105, i.e. within 1-2ms on the highest-value, highest-latency path, with 462 canary checkout requests and zero failures. The 4-window time series shows no degradation trend or late-breaking failure: canary p95 92, 92, 93, 96 and stable p95 94, 94, 95, 92, with 5xx at 0 in every window for both. Judgement: the 90-120s window where canary p95 (96) edges above stable (92) is a 4ms difference, inside the same noise band that stable itself moves across windows (92-95), and is not a monotonic climb, so I read it as measurement noise rather than warm-up damage, memory pressure, or a leak. Judgement on the one blemish: canary /browse p99 is 77ms vs stable 28ms. This is a genuine tail difference and the only asymmetry in the data, but I do not treat it as a release blocker because /browse p95 is identical at 27ms on both (so it is a thin slice of outlier requests, not a shifted distribution), and 77ms is still well below the service-wide p95 of 93ms and below normal /checkout p50, so no user crosses a meaningful latency threshold because of it. Residual risk I am accepting: a 120s test at 80 req/s with a single canary pod cannot rule out slow-burn problems (memory growth, connection-pool or cache exhaustion, cron/batch paths) or low-frequency error classes, and the /browse p99 outliers have no explanation yet. Mitigation: promote, then watch /browse p99, 5xx rate, and pod memory for the first period at 100% and roll back on any sustained regression. On the stated trade-off, a bad promote hurts customers, but there is no customer-visible harm in this data (zero errors, latency parity on all three endpoints including checkout), so blocking the release would not be supported by the evidence.
